INSIDE THE STUDY

A real Giulia mesh.
A defined flow model.

The scene uses a detailed existing Alfa Romeo Giulia asset with 1,161,110 triangles across 59 parts. It is not a generic sedan shape or an AI generated car. Materials have been adapted for browser rendering; the source does not include texture files.

How the air is calculated

The car mesh is converted into a sealed outer volume on a 136 × 48 × 72 grid. Two numerical potential flow solutions are calculated around that volume, with an impermeable body and slip ground. Their linear combination gives the selected wind angle; speed scales the field. Streamlines are integrated through this 3D velocity field.

Surface colors use the Bernoulli pressure coefficient, Cp = 1 − (local speed / freestream speed)². Click probes sample the fluid near the surface. The method assumes steady, inviscid, incompressible flow. It does not predict separation, a turbulent wake, viscous drag, or a real vehicle drag coefficient. The 100 mm grid cannot resolve every visible detail.

Experimental viscous flow

The optional wake solver runs locally in a background worker. It uses a D3Q19 lattice Boltzmann scheme with BGK collision, a static Smagorinsky closure, slip ground and stationary wheels. Reynolds number is reduced to 500 for this coarse grid. Pressure comes from density. This is an unvalidated experiment, not road-speed CFD; drag and lift are not reported. Each run ramps up from rest and stops after 4,000 steps. Hiding the window pauses calculation.
